tool.name: Jinja
tool.tagline: Fast, expressive Python template engine for HTML, config files and more
tool.description: Jinja is the template engine behind Flask, Ansible, dbt, Salt and many static site generators. Templates mix text with expressions, filters, loops, inheritance and macros, and are compiled to Python code for speed. Learning it pays off wherever you generate HTML, configuration or code from data.

glossary.def: A Python library for filling in text templates with data, used to produce web pages, emails, configuration files and more.
Jinja's central settings object: it knows where to find templates (its loader), whether to escape output, and which filters exist.
In Jinja, the part of an Environment that finds a template's text by its name, for example in a folder of files.
In Jinja, the set of variables a template can use while it is being rendered: the values you pass to render() plus global ones.
In Jinja, a function applied to a value with a vertical bar, like {{ name|upper }}, to transform it for display.
Jinja's setting that automatically makes every printed value safe to put in HTML, by rewriting characters like < and & as harmless codes.
Rewriting characters that have a meaning in HTML, such as < > & and quotes, as codes like < so a browser shows them as text instead of treating them as part of the page.
A code HTML uses to write a character safely, like < for < or & for &.
The object Jinja uses in place of a missing variable or attribute; by default it prints as nothing, while StrictUndefined raises an error instead.
In Jinja, a named region of a template, marked with {% block name %}...{% endblock %}, that child templates can replace.
Jinja's way of sharing a page layout: a base template marks blocks, and a child template extends it and fills in or replaces those blocks.
In Jinja, a reusable piece of template defined with {% macro %} that you call like a function, with arguments, to produce text.
A string type (from the MarkupSafe library) that Jinja treats as already-safe HTML, so it isn't escaped again.
Jinja's ways of removing the spaces and line breaks that template tags leave behind, with - markers or the trim_blocks and lstrip_blocks settings.
A Jinja feature that saves compiled templates to disk or a shared store, so a freshly started program doesn't have to compile them again.
The first step of compiling a template: it cuts the source text into small pieces called tokens, such as {{, a name or a |.
Abstract syntax tree: a tree of objects describing the structure of code (this loop contains this print of this variable), built by a parser.
Server-side template injection: an attack where someone gets to write template code that a server then runs, letting them reach things they shouldn't.
In Jinja, a class that adds new tags (template syntax) to an Environment, such as {% trans %} or {% break %}.

concepts.name: Environment, loaders and render
concepts.summary: Create a Jinja Environment with a loader, load templates by name, and fill them in with render().
concepts.why: Every use of Jinja goes through an Environment, and its settings decide escaping, where templates come from, and errors.
concepts.body: Think of a form letter: "Dear ___, your order ___ has shipped." The text stays the same; only the blanks change. A **template** is exactly that, text with placeholders, and filling the placeholders with real values to get the final text is called **rendering**. **Jinja** is a Python library for writing and rendering templates. The central object is the **`Environment`**. It holds the settings (such as escaping, covered below) and a **loader**, which finds templates by name, for example in a folder called `templates`: ```python env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader("templates"), autoescape=select_autoescape()) template = env.get_template("hello.html") html = template.render(name="Ann", items=[1, 2]) ``` `render()` takes keyword arguments or a single dict. Their names become the variables the template can use, together called the **context**. The result is a string. For huge outputs, `template.generate()` and `template.stream()` produce the text in pieces. For quick scripts, `Template("Hello {{ name }}!")` or `env.from_string(source)` makes a template from a string. For real projects, prefer one shared Environment with a loader: it keeps prepared templates ready for reuse, and lets templates in different files use each other. An important default: a bare `Environment()` has **autoescaping off**. Web pages are written in **HTML**, a text format where tags like `` and `` mark up the text. If a value containing `<` or `&` went into a page unchanged, the browser would read it as part of the page's code instead of as text. Rewriting those characters into harmless codes such as `<` is called **escaping**, and **autoescaping** does it for every value automatically. Off is right when the output isn't a web page, such as a text email or a settings file. For HTML you must turn it on, usually with `select_autoescape()`, which enables it for templates whose names end in `.html`, `.htm` or `.xml`. Flask, a popular library for building websites with Python, switches it on for you. Note that only the end of the name counts: `page.html.j2` is not escaped unless you pass `enabled_extensions=("html", "j2")` or similar. Template syntax has three kinds of markers. `{{ ... }}` prints the value of an **expression** (a piece of code that produces a value, like `price * 2`). `{% ... %}` runs a statement such as `if` or `for`. `{# ... #}` is a comment that produces no output.
concepts.code:
from jinja2 import DictLoader, Environment, Template, select_autoescape print(Template("Hello {{ name }}!").render(name="Ann")) # Hello Ann! env = Environment( loader=DictLoader({ # FileSystemLoader("templates") in real projects "greet.html": "

Hi {{ user }}{# not rendered #}

", "greet.txt": "Hi {{ user }}", }), autoescape=select_autoescape(), # on for .html/.htm/.xml ) print(env.get_template("greet.html").render(user="Bo")) #

Hi <b>Bo</b>

print(env.get_template("greet.txt").render({"user": "Bo"})) # Hi Bo
takeaways: An Environment holds config and a loader; get_template loads by name
render(**vars) or render(dict) returns a string
{{ }} prints, {% %} executes, {# #} comments
Environment() has autoescaping off; enable it for HTML
pitfalls: Rendering HTML with a default Environment(), leaving output unescaped.

quiz.q: What is the default autoescape setting of a plain Environment()?
options: On only for strings from users
quiz.explain: Autoescaping is off by default; select_autoescape() or autoescape=True turns it on.

concepts.name: Variables and expressions
concepts.summary: Print variables, read attributes and dict keys, write values directly, and use math, comparisons, joining and inline if.
concepts.why: Expressions are most of what templates contain, and their lookup rules explain many surprising blanks.
concepts.body:
Inside `{{ }}` you write **expressions**, which look a lot like Python:

- reading a value attached to an object or dict: `user.name` and `user["name"]` both work. A value attached to an object and read with a dot is an **attribute**. The dot form tries the attribute first, then the dict key; the bracket form tries the key first.
- values written out directly, called **literals**: strings, numbers, lists `[1, 2]`, dicts `{"a": 1}`, and `true`/`false`/`none` (Python's capitalised `True`, `False`, `None` work too)
- math: `+ - * / // % **`
- comparisons and logic: `== != < >= and or not in`
- `~` turns both sides into strings and joins them: `{{ "Item " ~ n }}`
- inline if: `{{ "yes" if ok else "no" }}`; the `else` is optional
- calling methods: `{{ name.upper() }}`, `{{ items|length }}` (that `|` is a filter, coming next)

Assign a variable with `{% set total = price * qty %}`.

**Missing values** are not errors by default. A missing variable, or a missing attribute or key on an existing object, becomes a special `Undefined` object that prints as an empty string. So a typo like `{{ user.nmae }}` silently renders nothing. One step further, reading an attribute of something that is itself missing (`{{ usr.name }}` when `usr` doesn't exist) raises `UndefinedError`. Later you'll see `StrictUndefined`, which makes every missing value an error, a good choice while developing and when generating configuration files.

Templates are meant to display data, not compute it. Jinja can call any method on what you pass in, so keep heavy logic in Python and hand templates values that are ready to show.
concepts.code:
from jinja2 import Template

t = Template("""{% set total = price * qty -%}
{{ user.name }} / {{ user["role"] }}
{{ "Order " ~ order_id }}: {{ qty }} x {{ price }} = {{ total }}
{{ "bulk" if qty >= 10 else "single" }}
{{ tags[0].upper() }} and {{ tags|length }} tags
[{{ user.nmae }}] typo renders empty""")

print(t.render(user={"name": "Ann", "role": "admin"}, order_id=7,
               qty=12, price=2.5, tags=["new", "sale"]))
# Ann / admin
# Order 7: 12 x 2.5 = 30.0
# bulk
# NEW and 2 tags
# [] typo renders empty
takeaways: a.b tries attribute then key; a["b"] tries key then attribute
~ joins values as strings; x if cond else y works inline
Missing values render as empty strings unless you use StrictUndefined
pitfalls: Hunting for minutes for the cause of a blank output when it was a misspelled variable.

quiz.q: user is a dict without an "emial" key. What does {{ user.emial }} render with default settings?
quiz.explain: A missing key on an existing object is Undefined, which prints as an empty string; only attribute access on an Undefined raises.

options: An error, you can't add str and int
quiz.explain: The ~ operator converts both operands to strings and concatenates them.

concepts.name: Filters and tests
concepts.summary: Transform values with filters like default, join, sort and map, and check values with tests like defined and divisibleby.
concepts.why: Filters let templates format data without Python code, and tests make conditions readable.
concepts.body:
A **filter** transforms a value. You write it after a vertical bar: `{{ name|title }}`. Filters chain left to right and can take arguments: `{{ items|sort(attribute="price")|join(", ") }}`.

Built-in filters you will use constantly:

- text: `upper`, `lower`, `title`, `capitalize`, `trim`, `truncate(30)`, `replace("a", "b")`, `wordwrap`, `striptags`
- fallback: `default("n/a")` (short form `d`); `default(x, true)` also replaces empty values and other values that count as false
- collections: `length`, `first`, `last`, `join`, `sort`, `unique`, `reverse`, `sum(attribute="price")`, `batch(3)`, `groupby("category")`, `dictsort`, `items`
- picking and pulling out: `map(attribute="name")` (the name of each item), `selectattr("active")` (only items whose `active` is true), `rejectattr("draft")`, `select("odd")`
- numbers and output: `round(2)`, `int`, `float`, `filesizeformat`, `format`, `tojson`, `e`, `safe`

`map`, `select` and their relatives don't give back a list. They produce items one at a time, only when asked, so print or reuse the result by finishing with `join`, `list` or `first`.

A **test** checks a value with `is`: `{% if user is defined %}`, `{% if n is divisibleby(3) %}`, `{% if x is none %}`, `is string`, `is number`, `is even`, `is iterable`, `is sameas(false)`. Negate with `is not`. Tests also power `select("odd")` and `selectattr("age", "ge", 18)` (age greater than or equal to 18).

Filters and tests are applied before most operators, so `{{ -3|abs }}` means `-(3|abs)`, which is -3. Use parentheses: `{{ (-3)|abs }}`.
concepts.code:
from jinja2 import Environment

env = Environment()
t = env.from_string("""{{ title|default("Untitled")|upper }}
{{ products|selectattr("in_stock")|map(attribute="name")|join(", ") }}
Total: {{ products|sum(attribute="price")|round(2) }}
{% for g in products|groupby("cat") %}{{ g.grouper }}={{ g.list|length }} {% endfor %}
{% for n in range(1, 7) if n is divisibleby(3) %}{{ n }} {% endfor %}
{{ bio|default("-", true) }} {{ note is defined }}""")

print(t.render(bio="", products=[
    {"name": "Pen", "price": 1.25, "cat": "office", "in_stock": True},
    {"name": "Ink", "price": 4.5, "cat": "office", "in_stock": False},
    {"name": "Mug", "price": 7.333, "cat": "kitchen", "in_stock": True}]))
# UNTITLED
# Pen, Mug
# Total: 13.08
# kitchen=1 office=2
# 3 6
# - False
takeaways: value|filter(args) transforms; filters chain left to right
default, join, sort, map, selectattr and groupby cover most formatting
Tests use is: is defined, is none, is divisibleby(n)
pitfalls: Forgetting that map and select don't return lists; finish with join, list or first.

quiz.explain: default only replaces undefined values unless the second argument (boolean) is true.

concepts.name: if, for and whitespace control
concepts.summary: Use if/elif/else, for loops with the loop variable and else, and strip whitespace with - markers or trim_blocks.
concepts.why: Lists and optional sections are the bread and butter of every template.
concepts.body:
`{% if %}` works like Python's, with `elif` and `else`, and is closed by `{% endif %}`.

`{% for item in items %}` loops over anything you can loop over in Python (a list, a dict, a string; such a value is called an **iterable**), and is closed by `{% endfor %}`. Inside the loop, the special **`loop`** variable gives:

- `loop.index` (counting from 1), `loop.index0` (from 0), `loop.revindex` (counting down)
- `loop.first`, `loop.last`, `loop.length`
- `loop.cycle("odd", "even")` for alternating values, `loop.previtem`, `loop.nextitem`, `loop.changed(value)`

Loop over dicts with `{% for key, value in d.items() %}`. Add a condition inline, `{% for u in users if u.active %}`, and `loop.length` counts only the matching items. An **`else`** block runs when the loop ran zero times: perfect for "No results".

There is no `break` or `continue` unless you switch on the `jinja2.ext.loopcontrols` extension. Also note that variables set inside a loop do **not** survive after it. To add things up across a loop, create a small object whose attributes you can change: `{% set ns = namespace(total=0) %}`, then `{% set ns.total = ns.total + x %}`.

**Whitespace control.** Tags leave their line breaks in the output, which matters when you generate text where layout counts, such as configuration files. Add `-` inside a marker to remove whitespace on that side: `{%- if x %}` strips before it, `{{ value -}}` after it.

Or set two options on the Environment: `trim_blocks=True` removes the first line break after a `{% %}` tag, and `lstrip_blocks=True` removes spaces before one. That pair is the usual choice for configuration files.
takeaways: loop.index, loop.first/last and loop.cycle are available in every for loop
for ... else handles empty lists; for x in xs if cond filters
Use namespace() to carry values out of a loop
- markers or trim_blocks/lstrip_blocks remove extra whitespace
pitfalls: Setting a variable inside a loop and expecting the change to be visible after it.

quiz.q: A template does {% set count = 0 %}{% for x in xs %}{% set count = count + 1 %}{% endfor %}{{ count }} with three items. What prints?
quiz.explain: Assignments inside the loop stay inside it; use a namespace object to add things up.

concepts.name: Template inheritance
concepts.summary: Build a base layout with blocks, extend it in child templates, call super(), and use required and scoped blocks.
concepts.why: Template inheritance gives every page the same layout without copy-pasting headers and footers.
concepts.body:
Most sites have one layout (header, menu, footer) and many pages that fill it in differently. **Template inheritance** handles that: a page template takes over a layout template and replaces just the parts it marks as replaceable. It is Jinja's most powerful layout tool.

A **base template** defines the page skeleton and marks replaceable regions as **blocks**:

```html
<title>{% block title %}My site{% endblock %}</title>
<main>{% block content %}{% endblock %}</main>
```

A **child template** starts with `{% extends "base.html" %}` and replaces only the blocks it needs. Anything in a child outside blocks is ignored, because the base decides the output.

Useful details:

- `{{ super() }}` renders the parent's version of the block, so a child can add to it rather than replace it, for example adding a script to a `scripts` block.
- Chains work: `page.html` extends `section.html`, which extends `base.html`; each level can replace blocks.
- `{% block sidebar required %}{% endblock %}` forces every child that gets rendered to fill it in.
- Blocks can't see variables defined in a surrounding `for` loop unless declared `scoped`: `{% block row scoped %}`.
- Reuse a block's content elsewhere with `{{ self.title() }}`, for example the title in both `<title>` and `<h1>`.
- Name the end tag for readability: `{% endblock content %}`.
- `extends` accepts a variable, so the layout can be chosen while rendering: `{% extends layout or "base.html" %}`.

A block can be defined only once per template, and `extends` should be the first tag. Keep base templates small and stable; pages change, the skeleton rarely does.
concepts.code:
from jinja2 import DictLoader, Environment env = Environment(loader=DictLoader({ "base.html": "{% block title %}Site{% endblock %}\n" "

{{ self.title() }}

\n" "
{% block content %}{% endblock %}
\n" "{% block scripts %}{% endblock %}", "post.html": "{% extends 'base.html' %}" "{% block title %}{{ post.title }} - {{ super() }}{% endblock %}" "{% block content %}{{ post.body }}{% endblock %}" "{% block scripts %}{% endblock %}" "This text is outside any block and never rendered.", }), autoescape=True) print(env.get_template("post.html").render(post={"title": "Hello", "body": "First post"})) # Hello - Site #

Hello - Site

#
First post
#
takeaways: A base template defines blocks; children extend it and replace blocks
super() includes the parent's block content
self.blockname() reuses a block; required forces children to fill it
pitfalls: Putting content outside blocks in a child template and wondering why it never appears.

quiz.q: In a child template, what does {{ super() }} inside a block do?
options: Renders the parent's content for this block
Calls the parent's macro of the same name
quiz.explain: super() outputs the block's content as defined one level up the inheritance chain.

concepts.name: Macros, include and import
concepts.summary: Write reusable macros with arguments and caller(), import them from other files, and include partial templates.
concepts.why: Repeated pieces of HTML, like form input boxes and cards, should be written once and used everywhere.
concepts.body:
A **macro** is a reusable piece of template that you call like a function:

```html
{% macro field(name, label, type="text", value="") %}
  <label>{{ label }} <input name="{{ name }}" type="{{ type }}" value="{{ value }}"></label>
{% endmacro %}
```

Call it like a function: `{{ field("email", "Email", type="email") }}`. Macros can have default arguments, and extra keyword arguments are available as `kwargs` if the macro mentions it.

A `{% call %}` block passes a chunk of template into a macro, which renders it with `{{ caller() }}`. That is how you write wrappers, such as cards or pop-up boxes, around any content.

To share macros across files:

- `{% import "forms.html" as forms %}` then `{{ forms.field(...) }}`
- `{% from "forms.html" import field, button as btn %}`

**Include** renders another template in place: `{% include "partials/nav.html" %}`. `ignore missing` skips files that don't exist, and a list tries each name in order.

The rules for which variables they see differ, which trips people up:

- `include` passes the **current context** by default, so the included template sees your variables.
- `import` does **not** pass the context by default, because Jinja keeps imported templates and reuses them. So macros in it can't see the page's variables unless you write `import ... with context`. Prefer passing values as macro arguments instead.

Rule of thumb: macros for components that take parameters, includes for fixed chunks like footers, template inheritance for the overall page layout.
takeaways: Macros are template functions with arguments and defaults
{% call %} + caller() pass a content block into a macro
include sees the current context; import doesn't unless with context
pitfalls: Expecting macros from an imported file to see the page's variables.

quiz.q: A macro in macros.html uses {{ user }}. It is imported with {% import "macros.html" as m %}. What does user render as?
options: Empty (undefined), because imports don't get the context by default
quiz.explain: Imported templates are rendered without the current context unless you add with context.

concepts.name: Autoescaping and safe markup
concepts.summary: Understand how autoescaping blocks cross-site scripting (XSS), when to use Markup and |safe, and how to output JSON for scripts.
concepts.why: Escaping mistakes in templates are a top cause of security holes in websites.
concepts.body: Imagine a comment box on a website. If someone types `` and your template puts that text into the page unchanged, every visitor's browser runs their JavaScript code. That attack is called **XSS** (cross-site scripting). With **autoescaping** on, every `{{ value }}` is escaped first: `<`, `>`, `&`, `"` and `'` become codes called **entities**, like `<`. Typed-in `
concepts.code:
from jinja2 import Environment from markupsafe import Markup env = Environment(autoescape=True) t = env.from_string("""

{{ comment }}

{{ trusted }}

{{ link }} """) print(t.render( comment="", trusted=Markup("{}").format("escaped arg"), url='x" onclick="evil()', link=Markup("Home"), user={"name": "
takeaways: Autoescaping escapes every {{ }} unless the value is Markup
Use |safe or Markup only for HTML you trust
Use |tojson for data inside <script>; always quote attribute values
pitfalls: Applying |safe to rich text from users without sanitizing it first.

quiz.q: How should you embed a Python dict as a JavaScript object inside a <script> tag?
quiz.explain: tojson emits valid JSON and escapes characters like < so the script tag cannot be closed early.

concepts.name: Custom filters, tests and globals
concepts.summary: Register your own filters, tests and global functions on the Environment, including context-aware ones with pass_context.
concepts.why: Your own formatting, such as money, dates or URL-friendly names, belongs in reusable filters, not repeated template code.
concepts.body:
When the built-ins aren't enough, add your own to the Environment. Filters, tests and globals live in three dicts of functions:

- `env.filters["money"] = format_money` makes `{{ price|money }}` call `format_money(price)`. Extra filter arguments become extra function arguments: `{{ price|money("EUR") }}` calls `format_money(price, "EUR")`.
- `env.tests["prime"] = is_prime` enables `{% if n is prime %}`.
- `env.globals["now"] = datetime.now` makes `{{ now() }}` available in every template; globals are also good for settings and helper functions.

Register them **before** loading templates. When Jinja first loads a template, it turns it into Python code (it **compiles** it), and filter names are looked up at that moment. So an unknown filter raises `TemplateAssertionError` when the template loads, rather than producing a blank later.

Sometimes a filter needs more than its value. Jinja provides **decorators** for this: the `@name` line written just above a `def`, which wraps the function. These pass an extra first argument:

- `@pass_context`: the active context, giving access to template variables, such as the user's language and region (their locale)
- `@pass_eval_context`: details of the current evaluation, mainly to check `eval_ctx.autoescape`
- `@pass_environment`: the Environment

A filter that returns HTML should return `Markup`, escaping its inputs, so it works correctly with autoescaping on. In Flask, register filters with `@app.template_filter()`, and globals with `@app.template_global()` or `@app.context_processor`.

Keep filters fast and free of side effects: they run for every value, on every render.
concepts.code: from decimal import Decimal from jinja2 import Environment, pass_context from markupsafe import Markup, escape def money(value, currency="USD"): return f"{Decimal(value):,.2f} {currency}" @pass_context def greet(ctx, name): # can read template variables return f"{ctx.get('greeting', 'Hello')}, {name}" def badge(text): return Markup('%s') % escape(text) env = Environment(autoescape=True) env.filters.update(money=money, greet=greet, badge=badge) env.tests["even_len"] = lambda s: len(s) % 2 == 0 env.globals["site"] = "Shop" t = env.from_string("{{ site }}: {{ 1234.5|money('EUR') }} | {{ 'Ann'|greet }} | " "{{ 'new'|badge }} | {{ 'abcd' is even_len }}") print(t.render(greeting="Hi")) # Shop: 1,234.50 EUR | Hi, Ann | <b>new</b> | True
takeaways: env.filters, env.tests and env.globals are dicts you can extend
Extra filter arguments map to extra function parameters
@pass_context gives a filter access to template variables
Return Markup from filters that produce HTML, escaping inputs
pitfalls: Registering a filter after templates using it were compiled, causing "No filter named" errors.

quiz.q: You register env.filters["slug"] = slugify. What does {{ title|slug("_") }} call?
quiz.explain: The filtered value is the first argument; filter arguments follow it.

concepts.name: Loaders, caching and auto-reload
concepts.summary: Pick the right loader (FileSystem, Package, Dict, Choice, Prefix), and understand template caching, auto_reload and bytecode caches.
concepts.why: Loader and cache setup decide where templates come from and how fast rendering is in a running application.
concepts.body:
The **loader** turns a template name into the template's text. Built-in options:

- `FileSystemLoader(["templates", "shared"])`: looks in these folders, in order
- `PackageLoader("myapp", "templates")`: loads from an installed Python package, ideal for libraries
- `DictLoader({...})`: templates held in a dict, great for tests
- `FunctionLoader(fn)`: any function that returns the text, for example reading it from a database
- `ChoiceLoader([a, b])`: tries loaders in order, so an app's templates can take precedence over a library's
- `PrefixLoader({"admin": loader})`: picks a loader by the first part of the name, as in `"admin/index.html"`

Template names always use forward slashes and can't climb out of the loader's folder with `..`.

**Caching.** `get_template` compiles a template once and keeps the result in a **cache**, a store of finished work kept for reuse (by default up to 400 templates, dropping the least recently used). With `auto_reload=True` (the default), Jinja checks on each `get_template` call whether the template file has changed and recompiles it if so. That's convenient while developing; in a live application, `auto_reload=False` skips those file checks.

**Bytecode cache.** Compiling is the expensive step. A **bytecode cache** (`FileSystemBytecodeCache`, or one based on memcached) saves compiled templates to disk. Then each newly started copy of your program, for example each of many short-lived worker processes, can skip recompiling.

`env.list_templates()` lists everything a loader can find. It's useful for compiling everything in advance, or for checking in your automated tests that every template is valid.

Keep **one Environment per application**. Creating a new Environment for every page request throws away the cache and recompiles every template each time, a common performance bug.
concepts.code:
import os, tempfile
from jinja2 import ChoiceLoader, DictLoader, Environment, FileSystemLoader, PrefixLoader

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    with open(os.path.join(d, "hello.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write("v1 from disk")
    env = Environment(loader=ChoiceLoader([
        FileSystemLoader(d),                                    # app templates win
        DictLoader({"hello.txt": "default", "footer.txt": "(c) lib"}),
        PrefixLoader({"admin": DictLoader({"index.txt": "admin home"})}),
    ]))
    print(env.get_template("hello.txt").render())        # v1 from disk
    print(env.get_template("footer.txt").render())       # (c) lib
    print(env.get_template("admin/index.txt").render())  # admin home
    print(env.get_template("hello.txt") is env.get_template("hello.txt"))  # True (cached)

    with open(os.path.join(d, "hello.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write("v2 edited")
    os.utime(os.path.join(d, "hello.txt"), (0, 10**10))   # make the change visible
    print(env.get_template("hello.txt").render())        # v2 edited (auto_reload)
takeaways: FileSystemLoader for apps, PackageLoader for libraries, ChoiceLoader to let app templates win
Compiled templates are cached; auto_reload re-checks the files
Use one shared Environment; a bytecode cache speeds up fresh starts
pitfalls: Creating a new Environment for every render, recompiling templates each time.

quiz.q: Why should a web app create its Jinja Environment once at startup?
options: Autoescaping only works on the first Environment
The Environment caches compiled templates, so reuse avoids recompiling
Loaders can only be attached once
quiz.explain: Compiling is the slow part; a shared Environment keeps compiled templates in its cache.

concepts.name: Undefined handling and debugging
concepts.summary: Choose Undefined, ChainableUndefined, DebugUndefined or StrictUndefined, and find which variables a template needs.
concepts.why: Silently empty output from a typo is a classic template bug, especially in config generation.
concepts.body:
When a template uses something that doesn't exist, Jinja creates an **undefined** object. Which kind is chosen on the Environment with `undefined=`:

- `Undefined` (default): prints as nothing, counts as false and loops as empty, but raises `UndefinedError` when you read an attribute from it (`{{ db.host }}` with no `db`) or do arithmetic with it
- `ChainableUndefined`: also allows `a.b.c` chains on missing values, giving undefined instead of raising, handy with deeply optional data
- `DebugUndefined`: prints the expression back, such as `{{ user.name }}`, so missing values stand out in the output
- `StrictUndefined`: raises `UndefinedError` on almost any use, including printing, looping and `if` checks

`StrictUndefined` is the safest choice for generated configuration files, emails and anything where a blank is a bug. With it, you can still handle optional values on purpose with `{% if x is defined %}` or `x|default("...")`, which work because tests and `default` don't trigger the error.

To find out which variables a template expects, have Jinja read its structure (`env.parse`) and ask:

```python
from jinja2 import meta
meta.find_undeclared_variables(env.parse(source))
```

That's useful for checking that the calling code provides everything, or for documenting what a template needs.

Error messages from Jinja include the template name and line number in the traceback, because Jinja remembers which template line each piece of its generated code came from.
concepts.code:
from jinja2 import ChainableUndefined, DebugUndefined, Environment, StrictUndefined, meta
from jinja2.exceptions import UndefinedError

src = "host={{ db_host }} port={{ port|default(5432) }} {% if debug is defined %}debug{% endif %}"

print(Environment().from_string(src).render())                 # host= port=5432
print(Environment(undefined=DebugUndefined).from_string(src).render())
# host={{ db_host }} port=5432
try:
    Environment(undefined=StrictUndefined).from_string(src).render()
except UndefinedError as e:
    print("error:", e)                                     # error: 'db_host' is undefined
print(Environment(undefined=StrictUndefined).from_string(src).render(db_host="h"))
# host=h port=5432
print(Environment(undefined=ChainableUndefined).from_string("[{{ a.b.c }}]").render())  # []

env = Environment()
print(sorted(meta.find_undeclared_variables(env.parse(src))))  # ['db_host', 'debug', 'port']
takeaways: The undefined= option decides what missing values do
StrictUndefined turns typos into errors; default and is defined still work
meta.find_undeclared_variables lists a template's inputs
pitfalls: Generating configuration files with the default Undefined, so a typo produces an empty value.

quiz.q: With StrictUndefined, what does {{ missing|default("x") }} render?
quiz.explain: The default filter checks for undefined without triggering the strict error.

concepts.name: How templates compile to Python
concepts.summary: Follow a template from source text to tokens, a syntax tree and generated Python code, and see how blocks, macros and context work.
concepts.why: Knowing the compiled form explains speed, which variables are visible where, and error tracebacks.
concepts.body:
Jinja doesn't read and act on a template line by line each time; it **compiles it to Python**, once. The steps:

1. The **lexer** cuts the source into small pieces called tokens (`{{`, a name, a `|`, plain text), using the configured markers. You can change `{{` and `{%` through Environment options.
2. The **parser** builds an **AST**, a tree of objects from `jinja2.nodes` (`Output`, `For`, `If`, `Name`, `Filter`, ...) describing the template's structure. `env.parse(source)` returns it; that's what `meta.find_undeclared_variables` looks at.
3. The **code generator** turns the AST into Python source code. You can read it with `env.compile(source, raw=True)`.
4. Python compiles that source into its own internal form, kept in memory and optionally in a bytecode cache.

In the generated code, the template body becomes a generator function `root(context, ...)` that yields strings, and each block becomes its own function in a `blocks` dict. That's why inheritance is cheap: when the parent's `root` runs, the child's block functions are used in place of the parent's. Macros become Python functions returning `Markup`.

Variables are looked up in the context: template variables first, then globals. Lookups are stored in local Python variables, so `{% set %}` inside a loop creates a new local variable that belongs to the loop. That's why assignments don't leak out of loops and blocks.

Filter and test names are looked up when the template is compiled, so an unknown filter fails as soon as the template loads, while undefined variables only matter when it renders.

Tracebacks point at template lines because Jinja keeps a map from generated lines back to template lines and rewrites the traceback.

The generated code is internal and changes between versions; read it to learn, never depend on it.
concepts.code:
from jinja2 import Environment
from jinja2.exceptions import TemplateAssertionError

env = Environment()
src = "{% for x in items %}{{ x|upper }}{% endfor %}"

print(env.parse(src))
# Template(body=[For(target=Name(name='x', ctx='store'), iter=Name(name='items', ...
code = env.compile(src, raw=True)
print([line for line in code.splitlines() if line.startswith("def ")])
# ['def root(context, missing=missing, environment=environment):']
print("t_1 = environment.filters['upper']" in code)          # True: resolved up front

try:
    env.from_string("{{ x|no_such_filter }}")              # fails at compile time
except TemplateAssertionError as e:
    print(e)                                                # No filter named 'no_such_filter'.
t = env.from_string("{{ x }}")
print(t.render(x=1), list(t.generate(x=2)))                 # 1 ['2']
takeaways: Templates go lexer -> parser AST -> generated Python -> Python's compiled form
Each template is a root() generator; blocks and macros become functions
Filters are looked up at compile time, variables at render time
pitfalls: Relying on the generated Python code, which is internal and changes between releases.

quiz.q: When is an unknown filter name in a template detected?
options: Only when that line is rendered
quiz.explain: Filters are looked up during code generation, so a missing one raises TemplateAssertionError at load time.

concepts.name: The sandboxed environment
concepts.summary: Render templates written by untrusted users with SandboxedEnvironment, and know what it does and doesn't protect against.
concepts.why: Letting users write templates (emails, themes, notifications) lets them run code on your server unless you sandbox it.
concepts.body:
If the template **text** itself comes from users, a normal Environment is dangerous. Jinja expressions can walk through Python's internals, for example `{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}`, and reach functions that read files or run commands on your server. This attack is **server-side template injection (SSTI)**.

`jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment` runs templates in a **sandbox**: a restricted mode that checks every attribute read and every call:

- underscore attributes such as `__class__` and `__globals__`, and Python's internal function and frame attributes, are blocked. They give a special undefined value that raises `SecurityError` as soon as it's used, and calling unsafe functions raises it too
- `range()` is capped (`MAX_RANGE`, 100000 items) to stop trivially huge loops
- `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment` also blocks methods that change lists, dicts and sets, like `append` or `update`

You can adjust the rules by subclassing and overriding `is_safe_attribute(obj, attr, value)` and `is_safe_callable(obj)`, or mark your own functions with `@unsafe` from the sandbox module.

What the sandbox does **not** do:

- stop a template from using up resources, with nested loops or huge strings. Enforce time limits and output size limits yourself, ideally by rendering in a separate process that you can stop.
- make unsafe objects safe: anything you put in the context can be reached. Pass plain data (dicts, strings, numbers), never database objects that have a `delete()` method, or your app's settings.
- escape output: autoescaping is still a separate setting.

The safest design is still not to let users write templates at all. If you must, combine the sandbox with minimal context data, autoescaping and resource limits.
concepts.code:
from jinja2.sandbox import ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment, SandboxedEnvironment
from jinja2.exceptions import SecurityError
from jinja2 import Environment

evil = "{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()|length > 0 }}"
print(Environment().from_string(evil).render())          # True: object graph reachable!

sandbox = SandboxedEnvironment(autoescape=True)
try:
    print(sandbox.from_string(evil).render())
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)                              # SecurityError

user_template = "Hi {{ user.name }}, you have {{ count }} new messages"
print(sandbox.from_string(user_template).render(user={"name": "Ann"}, count=3))
# Hi Ann, you have 3 new messages

immutable = ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment()
try:
    immutable.from_string("{{ items.append(4) }}").render(items=[1, 2, 3])
except SecurityError as e:
    print("blocked:", e)        # blocked: access to attribute 'append' of 'list' object is unsafe.
takeaways: SandboxedEnvironment blocks unsafe attributes and calls in untrusted templates
ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment also blocks methods that change lists, dicts and sets
The sandbox doesn't limit time or memory, and can't protect unsafe objects you pass in
pitfalls: Rendering template text supplied by users with a normal Environment (SSTI).

quiz.q: Which risk does SandboxedEnvironment NOT address on its own?
options: A template that loops a huge number of times to exhaust CPU
quiz.explain: The sandbox restricts attribute access and calls, but resource limits must be enforced separately.

concepts.name: Writing extensions and async rendering
concepts.summary: Add your own template tags with an Extension, use the built-in extensions, and render templates with async/await.
concepts.why: Extensions let you add new template syntax, such as caching or translation blocks, when filters and macros aren't enough.
concepts.body:
Filters, tests and globals extend what expressions can do. **Extensions** go further and add new **tags**, new `{% ... %}` syntax. Built-in ones are switched on by name:

```python
Environment(extensions=["jinja2.ext.i18n", "jinja2.ext.loopcontrols", "jinja2.ext.do"])
```

`i18n` adds `{% trans %}` blocks for translating text with gettext, `loopcontrols` adds `break` and `continue`, `do` runs an expression without printing it, and `debug` adds `{% debug %}` to print the whole context.

A custom extension subclasses `jinja2.ext.Extension`, declares `tags = {"mytag"}` and implements `parse(self, parser)`. The parser gives you the template's tokens one after another. You consume your tag, read arguments with `parser.parse_expression()`, collect the body with `parser.parse_statements(("name:endmytag",), drop_needle=True)`, and return AST nodes.

The most common pattern returns a `nodes.CallBlock` that calls a method on the extension via `self.call_method("_render", args)`. That method receives `caller`, a function that renders the body. This is how extensions that cache parts of a page work: compute a key, then return the saved output, or call `caller()` and save its result.

Extensions can also add attributes to the Environment with `self.environment.extend(...)`, and change the source text or the tokens before parsing.

**Async rendering.** Python's `async`/`await` lets code wait for slow things, like network calls, without holding everything else up. `Environment(enable_async=True)` compiles templates so they can wait on async functions and loop over async generators passed in the context. Render with `await template.render_async(...)`. It's useful when templates pull data from async sources, but it's slower than ordinary rendering, so prefer loading the data first and rendering the normal way.
concepts.code:
import asyncio
from jinja2 import Environment, nodes
from jinja2.ext import Extension

class ShoutExtension(Extension):
    tags = {"shout"}

    def parse(self, parser):
        lineno = next(parser.stream).lineno          # consume the "shout" token
        times = parser.parse_expression()            # {% shout 2 %}
        body = parser.parse_statements(("name:endshout",), drop_needle=True)
        return nodes.CallBlock(self.call_method("_render", [times]), [], [], body).set_lineno(lineno)
    def _render(self, times, caller):
        return (caller().strip().upper() + "! ") * times
env = Environment(extensions=[ShoutExtension, "jinja2.ext.loopcontrols"])
print(env.from_string("{% shout 2 %}hi {{ name }}{% endshout %}").render(name="ann"))
# HI ANN! HI ANN!
print(env.from_string("{% for i in range(9) %}{% if i > 2 %}{% break %}{% endif %}{{ i }}{% endfor %}").render())
# 012

async def get_user():
    return "Bo"
aenv = Environment(enable_async=True)
print(asyncio.run(aenv.from_string("Hello {{ get_user() }}").render_async(get_user=get_user)))
# Hello Bo
takeaways: Built-in extensions: i18n, loopcontrols, do, debug
A custom tag = an Extension subclass with tags and parse() returning AST nodes
CallBlock + call_method lets Python code wrap a rendered body
enable_async + render_async let templates await async functions
pitfalls: Writing an extension for something a filter, global or macro could do more simply.

quiz.q: In an extension's _render(self, ..., caller) method, what does caller() return?
options: The name of the calling template
The template source of the tag body
The rendered output of the tag's body
quiz.explain: CallBlock passes a caller function that renders the body between the opening and end tags.
